beats.beat: Specialty chemicals are sold for what they do, not what they contain — a buyer adds one to a paint, plastic, textile or construction mix to change a specific property. The filing groups the company's range into Functional Additives (FA), Chemically Modified Minerals (CMM), Soft Minerals (SM) and Hard Minerals (HM).

The company's own description is that it is engaged in processing and selling this wide range of specialty chemicals, with a long-term arrangement for its corporate promoter to market and sell the products through the promoter's network.

The filing lists its strengths as a diversified product portfolio, diversified user industries, import substitution, support of the holding company, product innovation and R&D, and a strong management team.

Sales are not locked in by contracts: the company has not entered into long-term or definitive agreements with customers and relies on purchase orders to govern volume, pricing and other terms. It also has no long-term agreements with raw material suppliers.
Customer concentration is high: the top 10 customers accounted for around 59%, 57% and 59% of revenue from operations in FY2015, FY2016 and FY2017.
Exports have been a modest part of the story: about ₹10.68 crore of exports over the five years to the DRHP, going to Nigeria, Saudi Arabia and Sri Lanka.

Operating footprint: the company manufactures at Plot 347, GIDC Waghodia, Vadodara, Gujarat and Plot 104/3, Thenkasi Road, Pathur Village, Tirunelveli, Tamil Nadu, with administrative offices in Bhuj and Udaipur. None of these premises are owned by the company.

beats.beat: Restated financials are the company's past accounts realigned to common accounting policies, so figures are comparable across years. The DRHP presents six periods: the six months ended 30 September 2017 and the five financial years from FY2013 to FY2017.

Profit after tax turned positive from FY2015. It was a loss of ₹0.27 crore in FY2013 and ₹0.12 crore in FY2014, then a profit of ₹1.50 crore in FY2015, ₹0.90 crore in FY2016 and ₹1.75 crore in FY2017. The first half of FY2018 earned ₹1.33 crore.
Basic earnings per share followed the same arc: ₹(0.45) in FY2013, ₹(0.20) in FY2014, ₹2.47 in FY2015, ₹1.46 in FY2016, ₹2.43 in FY2017 and ₹1.48 in the six months ended 30 September 2017.

Operating cash flow is more volatile than profit: an inflow of ₹8.03 crore in FY2016 swung to an outflow of ₹3.50 crore in FY2017, before returning to an inflow of ₹1.25 crore in the first half of FY2018. The filing itself flags that the company has had negative cash flows in previous years and warns that sustained negative cash flow could affect growth.
Total assets were ₹34.25 crore at 30 September 2017, compared with ₹30.19 crore at 31 March 2013, ₹25.93 crore at 31 March 2015 and ₹27.67 crore at 31 March 2016. The movement is not a straight line.
What is missing: the excerpted pages do not include the revenue from operations line for the reported periods. The report will flag this rather than guess at the top-line trend.

beats.beat: Four promoters are named: Mr. Chandresh S. Parikh, Mr. Atil C. Parikh, Mr. Rajesh C. Parikh, and 20 Microns Limited as the corporate promoter.

Ownership is almost total: promoters hold 89,48,270 equity shares, or 99.76% of the pre-issue paid-up equity share capital. The promoter group, excluding the promoters, holds another 21,510 shares, or 0.24%.

As at 30 September 2017, the company's authorised share capital was ₹2,000 lakh, comprising 20,000,000 equity shares of ₹10 each; the issued, subscribed and paid-up capital was ₹897 lakh, or 89,70,000 equity shares.

Related-party transactions are a flagged issue: the company has entered into them over the past five financial years and the six months ended 30 September 2017, and the DRHP says there is no assurance they will not have an adverse effect on financial condition or results.

Compliance hygiene has been imperfect: there have been instances of non-filing, incorrect filing or delays in filing statutory forms with the Registrar of Companies, later filed with additional fees. The company also says it has not yet obtained registration for its corporate logo.
The company, its promoters, group company and directors are parties to legal proceedings, and the DRHP warns that adverse decisions could have a material effect on operations and finances.
Premises are not owned: the two manufacturing facilities and the Bhuj and Udaipur administrative offices sit on properties the company does not own, another item the filing lists as an internal risk.

beats.beat: The DRHP positions specialty chemicals as a growth slice of a much larger chemicals market. The Indian chemicals industry, excluding pharmaceuticals and fertilisers, was estimated at ₹5,800–6,200 billion in fiscal 2017; specialty chemicals (other than agrochemicals and dyestuff) made up about 17% of that, around ₹1,000 billion.
Growth has been strong and is expected to stay strong: the specialty chemicals segment grew at 10–12% CAGR from fiscal 2014 to 2017, and CRISIL Research forecasts 12–14% CAGR going forward.

The fastest-growing end-markets named in the filing are construction chemicals, water chemicals and personal care ingredients, each expected to grow at 15% CAGR; surfactants at 13%; and textile chemicals and flavours & fragrances at 12%.

Demand drivers cited include a growing Indian middle class, improved consumption standards, a Draft National Chemical Policy aimed at raising the chemicals sector's share of GDP, 100% FDI in the sector, and China's stricter environmental rules since 2015, which have reduced its chemical output and opened space for others.

Competition is fragmented: SMEs hold 70–75% of the specialty chemicals market, and only a few Indian players have the scale or capability to compete with global giants on product development and innovation.
The filing also names a headwind: from 2012-13 to 2016-17, chemicals imports grew at a faster pace (6.4% CAGR) than exports (6% CAGR), and exports to the EU face strict REACH regulation.
Two downstream markets are sized in the DRHP: the domestic paints industry at roughly ₹401 billion in fiscal 2017, and the organised cosmetics and toiletries market at ₹430–460 billion.

beats.beat: 20 Microns Nano Minerals is a Vadodara-based processor and seller of specialty chemicals that are grouped into four families: functional additives, chemically modified minerals, soft minerals and hard minerals.
It does not sell into the market on its own; a long-term arrangement with its corporate promoter, 20 Microns Limited, markets and sells its products through the promoter's network.

The DRHP is for a listing on the SME platform of NSE, called NSE EMERGE; the stated objects of the issue include funding a new manufacturing facility at GIDC Waghodia in Vadodara, Gujarat, and general corporate purposes.
The issue is managed by Vivro Financial Services Private Limited as lead manager, with Link Intime India Private Limited as registrar.

beats.beat: Customer concentration without contracts: the top 10 customers have accounted for roughly 57–59% of revenue from operations across three straight years, and sales are governed only by purchase orders, with no long-term customer agreements in place.

Cash flow can turn negative even in profit years: operating cash flow was an outflow of ₹3.50 crore in FY2017 despite a profit of ₹1.75 crore, and the DRHP warns that negative cash flows in earlier years could impact growth and business.

One plant is not fully licensed: the manufacturing facility at Plot 9-10, GIDC Waghodia, Vadodara is operating without certain statutory and regulatory licences and approvals, and the company says it cannot assure it will not be penalised for the non-compliance.

The business model depends on the corporate promoter: a long-term arrangement with 20 Microns Limited handles marketing and sales of its products, and the company has a history of related-party transactions that the DRHP says could have an adverse effect.

Currency exposure is real: with exports to Nigeria, Saudi Arabia and Sri Lanka, the company is exposed to foreign-exchange fluctuations that the DRHP says could harm results of operations, impact cash flows and cause financial results to fluctuate.
